title: Proximity: space makes groups
summary: See how your brain groups what it sees, and use spacing alone to show what belongs together.
objective: Use spacing to group related items: less space inside a group than between groups.

hook.prompt: Nothing connects these nine dots, and they're all the same. What do you see first?

visual.html: <svg viewBox='0 0 272 40' direction='ltr' class='w-full max-w-xs mx-auto' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='16' cy='20' r='7' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='36' cy='20' r='7' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='56' cy='20' r='7' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='116' cy='20' r='7' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='136' cy='20' r='7' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='156' cy='20' r='7' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='216' cy='20' r='7' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='236' cy='20' r='7' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='256' cy='20' r='7' class='fill-foreground'/></svg>
visual.alt: Nine identical dots in a row: three close together, a wide gap, three more, a wide gap, and three more.

options.feedback: That's what's on the screen, but most people don't see it that way at first glance.
The dots do sit in one line, yet most people see it break into pieces.

hook.explanation: Most people see three groups, though no line or box draws them. Only the gaps differ. So why does your brain make groups at all?

bricks.title: Your brain sees wholes first
bricks.body: Your eyes take in countless separate bits: dots, edges, colours. Your brain doesn't list them one by one. It quickly organises them into **wholes**: groups, shapes, and objects. Early in the 1900s, German psychologists named this **Gestalt**, meaning "shape" or "form". Look at the picture: twelve separate dots, yet you see one ring.

term.definition: Rules describing how the brain organises separate things it sees into groups and whole shapes.

visual.html: <svg viewBox='0 0 120 120' direction='ltr' class='w-32 mx-auto' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='105' cy='60' r='6' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='99' cy='82.5' r='6' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='82.5' cy='99' r='6' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='60' cy='105' r='6' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='37.5' cy='99' r='6' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='21' cy='82.5' r='6' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='15' cy='60' r='6' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='21' cy='37.5' r='6' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='37.5' cy='21' r='6' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='60' cy='15' r='6' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='82.5' cy='21' r='6' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='99' cy='37.5' r='6' class='fill-foreground'/></svg>
visual.alt: Twelve separate dots arranged evenly around a circle, so they read as one ring.

bricks.prompt: These are just two dots and a curve, and they don't touch. Why do most people see a face?

visual.html: <svg viewBox='0 0 120 110' direction='ltr' class='w-28 mx-auto' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='42' cy='40' r='7' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='78' cy='40' r='7' class='fill-foreground'/><path d='M34 68 Q60 96 86 68' fill='none' stroke-width='6' stroke-linecap='round' class='stroke-foreground'/></svg>
visual.alt: Two dots side by side above an upward curve, not touching each other.

options.text: The brain organises separate parts into one whole
The parts are joined into one shape
options.feedback: Look again: nothing touches. The joining happens in your brain, not on the screen.

options.text: We look at each part on its own, then add them up
options.feedback: That's the step the brain skips. It jumps straight to the whole, before listing the parts.

bricks.hint: Is the face on the screen, or in how you see it?
bricks.explanation: The screen shows three loose parts. Your brain groups them into one familiar whole, a face, before you notice the parts.

bricks.title: Proximity: near means together
bricks.body: The first Gestalt principle is **proximity**: things close together look like one group, and wider gaps separate groups. What counts is the *difference* in spacing. A dot joins the neighbours closer to it than the rest. If every gap is the same, nothing groups. Below, the dots are identical; only the spacing changes, and so does what you see.

term.definition: The Gestalt principle that things placed close together are seen as one group.

visual.html:
Closer side to side: rows
Closer top to bottom: columns
visual.alt: Two dot grids. In one, dots sit closer side to side and read as rows; in the other, closer top to bottom and read as columns.

bricks.prompt: How many groups do these sixteen dots form?

visual.html: <svg viewBox='0 0 92 92' direction='ltr' class='w-28 mx-auto' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='10' cy='10' r='5' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='26' cy='10' r='5' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='66' cy='10' r='5' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='82' cy='10' r='5' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='10' cy='26' r='5' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='26' cy='26' r='5' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='66' cy='26' r='5' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='82' cy='26' r='5' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='10' cy='66' r='5' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='26' cy='66' r='5' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='66' cy='66' r='5' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='82' cy='66' r='5' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='10' cy='82' r='5' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='26' cy='82' r='5' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='66' cy='82' r='5' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='82' cy='82' r='5' class='fill-foreground'/></svg>
visual.alt: Sixteen dots in a square, with a wider gap running across the middle and another running down the middle.

options.feedback: The two wide gaps through the middle break the block apart. Wider gaps separate groups.
There's a wide gap running across *and* one running down, so the square splits twice.

bricks.hint: Find where the gaps are wider than the rest.
bricks.explanation: One wide gap runs across and one runs down. Dots on the same side of both gaps are closest, so they form four groups of four.

bricks.prompt: You want these eight dots to read as two groups of four. Which change does it?

visual.html: <svg viewBox='0 0 200 24' direction='ltr' class='w-full max-w-xs mx-auto' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='16' cy='12' r='6' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='40' cy='12' r='6' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='64' cy='12' r='6' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='88' cy='12' r='6' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='112' cy='12' r='6' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='136' cy='12' r='6' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='160' cy='12' r='6' class='fill-foreground'/><circle cx='184' cy='12' r='6' class='fill-foreground'/></svg>
visual.alt: Eight identical dots in a row, all evenly spaced.

options.text: Widen the gap between the fourth and fifth dots
Spread all the dots further apart
options.feedback: Bigger gaps that are all equal still give one even row. Proximity needs some gaps to differ from others.

options.text: Move all the dots closer together
options.feedback: A tighter row is still one row, because every dot is just as near its neighbours as before.

bricks.hint: Grouping comes from differences in spacing, not the spacing itself.
bricks.explanation: One wider gap in the middle leaves each set of four closer to each other than to the other set, so the row splits in two.

bricks.title: Proximity on screens
bricks.body: Screens use proximity everywhere. Put a label right next to the field it names, then leave a bigger gap before the next label. The rule: **less space inside a group than between groups**. When all the gaps are equal, the screen blurs into one long list, and people can't tell what belongs to what. Here, each label clearly sits with its own field.

visual.alt: A sign-up form: Full name, Email, and Password labels each sit just above their own field, with larger gaps between the pairs.

bricks.prompt: Which form makes it clearer which label goes with which field?

visual.alt: A form with Name, Phone, and City labels, each placed exactly halfway between the field above and the field below.

options.feedback: Each label sits as close to the field above as to its own, so it could belong to either.

visual.alt: A form with Name, Phone, and City labels, each placed just above its own field, with bigger gaps between the pairs.

bricks.hint: Look at the gap above each label and the gap below it.
bricks.explanation: Each label is much closer to its own field than to the one above, so every label and field read as a pair.

bricks.prompt: Each caption is meant to sit under its own photo. Tap the caption that looks like it belongs to the wrong photo.

visual.html:
Photo 1

Lake at sunrise

Photo 2

Mountain trail

bricks.hint: Which photo is each caption closest to?
bricks.explanation: **Lake at sunrise** sits far below Photo 1 and almost touching Photo 2, so it reads as Photo 2's caption.

challenge.situation: On this checkout page, people keep typing their billing address into the shipping fields. Every label, field, and heading is spaced the same.

visual.html:
Shipping address

Billing address
visual.alt: A checkout form with Shipping address and Billing address headings, each followed by Street and ZIP code fields, all evenly spaced.

options.text: Pull each label close to its field, and leave a much bigger gap between the shipping and billing sections
options.outcome: Labels pair with their fields, and the two sections read as separate groups. Fewer people type into the wrong one.

options.text: Make both headings bigger and bolder, but keep the spacing even
options.outcome: The headings stand out more, but each one sits as close to the field above as to the fields below, so the form still scans as one long list.

options.text: Spread every element further apart so the page feels less crowded
options.outcome: The page looks airier, but all the gaps are still equal, so nothing groups and the mix-ups continue.

challenge.hint: Grouping comes from gaps that differ, at two levels: label to field, and section to section.
challenge.explanation: Proximity needs uneven spacing: tight inside each pair and each section, wide between sections. Bigger headings or bigger equal gaps don't create groups.

takeaways: Your brain groups what it sees into wholes before it notices the separate parts.
Proximity: things close together look like one group, and wider gaps separate groups.
On screens, leave less space inside a group than between groups, so people see what belongs together.
